    Timing diagram & logic analyser

    The circuit above, drawn over time. Give each input a drive pattern (a repeating string of 0s and 1s), then run steps: every step applies the next pattern bit to every input and records the settled outputs. The strip is drawn from those recorded simulation steps — it is a logic-analyser view of the same trace. In breadboard view the nodes are the full adder's nets.

    Analyser nodes — tick what to draw
    Details — reading a chronogram

    Time runs left to right; each row is one wire. A trace rides the top of its row for 1 and the bottom for 0. Vertical edges are the moments a value changes. For combinational circuits each step settles instantly, so the strip shows one settled sample per step; for the sequential pack below, each step is one clock period and you can watch state change only on edges.

    Karnaugh map & Boolean minimiser

    Tap a cell to cycle 0 → 1 → X (don't care). The minimiser (Quine–McCluskey) finds a smallest sum-of-products covering your 1-cells, draws the groups, and counts the gates. The table at the right edits the same function from the other side.

    Minimal sum of products
    Product of sums (Advanced)
    Truth table — tap the F cell to edit
    The minimised expression, built on the site engine — flip the inputs
    Details — reading a K-map

    Neighbouring cells — including wrap-around neighbours at the edges — differ in exactly one variable (Gray-code order: 00, 01, 11, 10). A group of 2, 4, 8 or 16 adjacent 1-cells is one product term; the variables that stay constant across the group are the ones that survive in the term. Bigger group = fewer literals = cheaper hardware. Don't-care cells (X) may join a group when that makes the group bigger, but never have to be covered.

    Details — latch vs flip-flop, and why the clock matters

    A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable is high it is transparent and the output follows the input. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it copies its input at one instant — the rising clock edge — and holds it otherwise. Counters, shift registers and RAM are all built from flip-flops sharing one clock, which is what keeps a whole machine changing state in lockstep instead of racing.

    Arduino Uno — pins at a glance

    A microcontroller board: the ATmega328P chip runs one program in a loop. Pins are grouped by job — the ~ mark means the pin can do PWM (analogWrite).

    Digital D0–D13 — on/off in or out. D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11 carry ~ : PWM.

    Analog A0–A5 — measure voltages 0–5 V as numbers 0–1023.

    Power — 5V and 3.3V out, GND, Vin to feed the board 7–12 V.

    Watch out: a pin can source only about 20 mA safely — enough for one LED with a resistor, never a motor directly.

    Raspberry Pi — board & 40-pin GPIO header

    A full tiny computer: SoC, RAM, USB and Ethernet, booting from microSD. The 40-pin header mixes power, ground and signal pins — the groups matter more than memorising numbers.

    Power — 3.3V (pins 1, 17) and 5V (pins 2, 4) rails. Ground — eight GND pins spread along the header.

    GPIO — general-purpose 3.3 V signals you set from code. I2C — GPIO2/3 (SDA/SCL). SPI — GPIO10/9/11 with CE on 8/7. UART — GPIO14/15 (TXD/RXD).

    Watch out: Pi pins are 3.3 V logic and not 5 V tolerant — 5 V into a GPIO pin can kill the board.

    Project 1 · LED on a breadboard

    Beginner

    An LED with no resistor dies fast. Size the current-limiting resistor with Ohm's law, live.

    Teaches: Ohm's law in a real loop, forward voltage, E12 standard values.

    You need: LED, resistor (value computed below), breadboard, jumper wires, a DC supply.

    Project 2 · Arduino PWM dimmer

    Beginner

    analogWrite does not lower the voltage — it chops it. The LED is fully on or fully off, thousands of times a second; your eye averages it.

    void setup() { pinMode(9, OUTPUT); }
void loop() {
  int v = analogRead(A0) / 4;  // 0..255
  analogWrite(9, v);           // PWM on D9
}

    Teaches: duty cycle, analogWrite, why PWM dims LEDs and drives motors.

    You need: Arduino Uno, LED, 220 Ω resistor, potentiometer, breadboard.

    Project 3 · Raspberry Pi GPIO control

    Beginner+

    Click a GPIO pin on the virtual header to drive it HIGH or LOW. The LED on the mini breadboard follows, and the Python updates with it.

    import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
GPIO.setup(17, GPIO.OUT)
GPIO.output(17, GPIO.LOW)
    GPIO17 is LOW — LED off.

    Teaches: BCM pin numbering, GPIO setup/output, 3.3 V logic levels.

    You need: Raspberry Pi, LED, 220 Ω resistor, breadboard, two jumper wires.

    Intermediate

    The same full adder from the circuits area — with no gates at all. Two LUTs hold the answers.

    Applied systems — bigger demos

    Project 5 · Traffic light controller

    Intermediate

    A finite-state machine you can watch think. Block flow: timer + pedestrian button → state machine → lamp decoder → lights.

    State table — current state highlighted

    Same idea as the circuits area

    Underneath, this controller is a counter plus a decoder: a state register steps through codes and each lamp is a logic function of the state bits — gates from the Gate Lab, nothing more. The four road phases ride a 2-bit cycle:

    Clearance (all-red) and WALK states extend the register to 3 bits — real controllers do exactly this: more states, wider counter, same decode idea.

    Teaches: finite-state machines, counters + decoders, why all-red clearance exists, input requests handled at safe points.

    You need (microcontroller build): Arduino, 6 LEDs + 6 resistors, pushbutton, breadboard. Pure-logic build: 555 timer or clock source, 2-bit counter IC (e.g. 74LS93), AND/OR/NOT gates to decode the lamps.

    Project 6 · Soil monitoring & irrigation

    Intermediate

    Sense → decide → act → report. Block flow: capacitive probe → microcontroller → display + relay/pump, with radio reports onward.

    Sun dries the soil over time; the pump fights back when moisture drops below threshold.
    Sensing chain
    Capacitive sensorin the soil; its capacitance rises with water content — no corroding probes
    ↓ reads as a voltage / count
    MicrocontrollerESP32 or Arduino class — compares moisture with the threshold
    ↓ decides
    Display + relayOLED shows the reading; the relay switches the pump
    ↓ reports
    Radio reportreadings are sent onward (e.g. LoRa) — how field plots and underground or remote sensors phone home

    Teaches: sensor thresholds and hysteresis, closed-loop control (the pump changes the thing it measures), relays switching bigger loads, telemetry.

    You need: capacitive soil-moisture sensor, ESP32 or Arduino, relay module, small pump, OLED display, battery or small solar panel for field use.

    Project 7 · Automatic night light

    Beginner

    Sensor → comparator → lamp. An LDR in a voltage divider watches the light; when the divider voltage says “dark”, a transistor switches the lamp on. This is the divider + transistor pair from the components library, working.

    Teaches: voltage dividers, comparators, transistors as switches.

    You need: LDR, 10 kΩ resistor, NPN transistor (2N2222), LED + resistor, 5 V supply.

    Project 8 · Water tank level controller

    Beginner+

    Three float switches, pure gate logic — decoded by this site's own netlist engine. Fill until FULL, warn when EMPTY.

    Teaches: float switches, combinational decode, lamps and interlocks from raw logic.

    You need: 3 float switches, NOT + AND gates (or one Arduino), pump relay, FULL/EMPTY LEDs.

    Logic levels — when is a voltage a 1?

    A bit is not a thing: it is a voltage agreed to be high or low, and modulation is how that agreement gets onto a wave. Drag the voltage and see what each logic family makes of it.

    Bonus · QPSK constellation

    QPSK sends two bits per symbol by picking one of four phases. Your pattern, paired up:

    Gray-coded: neighbours differ by one bit, so a small phase error usually costs only one bit.

    Why four schemes?

    NRZ-L is what happens on a wire between chips. ASK, FSK and BPSK put the same bits onto a carrier so they can travel — radio, cable, fibre. What the receiver can still tell apart after noise and distance is the whole game: that is exactly what the “watch out” line under each scheme is about.

    Bench tools: every number below is computed live from the values you set — change an input and the result, the diagram and the substituted formula all move together.

    Number-conversion trainer

    Random challenges between binary, decimal and hex. Type the answer, get checked instantly — miss, and the worked conversion is shown, not just the answer.

    —
    Details — how conversions work

    Binary → decimal: add each bit × its place value (…, 8, 4, 2, 1). Decimal → binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders upward, or subtract descending powers of two. Hex is base 16 with digits 0–9 then A–F; each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so binary ↔ hex converts in nibbles with no arithmetic.

    Voltage divider

    Tool

    Two resistors in series split a voltage in proportion to their values.

    Details

    Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). The same current flows through both resistors, so the drop across each is proportional to its resistance. Loading Vout with a low resistance pulls it down — a divider is a reference, not a power supply.

    RC time constant

    Tool

    How fast a capacitor charges through a resistor: one τ reaches 63% of the final voltage.

    Details

    τ = R × C (seconds, with C in farads). Charging toward 5 V: V(t) = 5(1 − e^(−t/τ)) — 63.2% at t = τ, 95% at 3τ, 99.3% at 5τ. Discharging is the mirror: V(t) = 5·e^(−t/τ), down to 36.8% at τ.

    RC low-pass filter

    Tool

    Passes slow signals, fades fast ones. The cutoff fc is where the output falls to 70.7% (−3 dB).

    Details

    fc = 1 / (2πRC). Magnitude |H(f)| = 1 / √(1 + (f/fc)²): 1.0 well below fc, 0.707 at fc, and falling at −20 dB per decade above it. This is the same RC pair as the time-constant tool, seen in frequency instead of time: fc = 1/(2πτ).

    555 astable designer

    Tool

    The classic free-running oscillator: two resistors and a capacitor set the blink rate and the on/off split.

    Details

    The capacitor charges through R1 + R2 and discharges through R2 alone, between ⅓ and ⅔ of the supply: t_high = 0.693(R1 + R2)C, t_low = 0.693·R2·C, f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2R2)C), duty = (R1 + R2)/(R1 + 2R2) — always above 50% in this classic circuit.

    ADC visualiser

    Tool

    An analog-to-digital converter slices a voltage range into 2^N steps. More bits = finer steps = smaller quantisation error.

    Details

    Reference 5 V. Step size (1 LSB) = 5 / 2^N volts. The converter outputs code = floor(Vin / LSB), capped at 2^N − 1; reading the code back as the step's midpoint, (code + ½)·LSB, keeps the quantisation error within ±½ LSB. The staircase drawn is the converter's transfer function: flat treads are the voltages that share one code.

    Overflow — when add traps and addu wraps

    A 32-bit register holds a fixed range of values, and adding 1 to the largest signed value, 0x7FFFFFFF, leaves that range. Real MIPS answers the same addition two different ways, depending on one letter: addu wraps the result around modulo 232 and carries on without a word; add raises an overflow exception — a trap — and halts instead of writing a wrong answer. Same numbers below, both times: only the instruction changes. Each demo runs in the lab's own simulator above — press Run, watch the register file, then read the machine's own numbers underneath.

    Wrap-around — addu rolls over

    
            
            
    
          
    
          
    
            
    Trap — add refuses
    
            
    
            
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Why it matters
    
          
    Wrap-around is silent. Nothing announces that the answer is wrong, so the wrapped value flows onward as if it were true. A counter or timer rolls over while the system around it assumes it only grows. The Year 2038 problem is exactly this: the 32-bit signed counter of seconds since 1970 wraps, and dates jump back to 1901. And in security work the dangerous version is a size calculation that wraps small — code checks that length + header fits the buffer, the addition wraps past 232 back to a small number, the check passes, and the copy that follows writes far past the end of the buffer. A trap is the opposite failure style: the machine stops loudly, at the exact instruction that overflowed, before the bad value can be used anywhere. Neither behaviour is itself the bug — the bug is not knowing which one your instruction does.
    
          
    C draws the same line, and it is the rule from your programming course: unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition — C's unsigned int behaves like addu — while signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so a C compiler may assume it never happens. That is why the u-variants exist for addresses and bit patterns, where wrap-around is the arithmetic you actually mean, and the trapping forms are the default for values, where an overflow means the program is wrong and you want to know immediately.

    Write policy — write-through vs write-back (Advanced)
    
          
    Reads fill lines; writes are where the policies split. Run a write below and watch the dirty bit: write-through updates memory on every write (dirty never sets, memory traffic on every write); write-back marks the line dirty and only writes memory back when the line is evicted (less traffic, but memory is stale until then — crash before eviction and the newest data is lost).

    Disk scheduling — FCFS vs SCAN
    
        
    Tracks 0–199. The SCAN here sweeps toward higher tracks servicing on the way, then reverses after the highest request (technically LOOK behaviour — it does not travel to track 199 for nothing). The path drawn and the total are computed from the same order, so they always agree.
    
        
    
          
          
          
          
        
    
        
    
        
    
      
    

      
    
        
    Deadlock & Banker's algorithm
    
        
    Edit what each process holds (Allocation) and the most it may still claim (Max). Available = Total − everything allocated. The safety check runs the real Banker's algorithm: it repeatedly looks for a process whose remaining Need fits in Available, lets it finish, and takes its Allocation back. If every process can finish in some order, the state is safe — that order is shown. If the search stalls, the state is unsafe: deadlock is possible from here, even if it has not happened yet.
    
        
    
          
          
          
          
        
    
        
    
        
    Press “Run safety check”.
    
        
    Details — the resource-allocation graph of this state
          
    Circles are processes, squares are resource types (label = units free). An arrow resource → process means “holds units of it”; process → resource means “still needs units of it”. A cycle of wanting is not required for an unsafe state — that is exactly why the Banker's check exists.
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Make it deadlock — circular wait
    
          
    Four processes, four single-unit resources. Each process holds one resource and waits for the next one round the ring: a perfect circular wait, so nobody can ever move. Break it by making one process release its resource — the whole ring then unwinds in order.
    
          
    
          
    
            
            
            
          
    
          
    Deadlocked: P0 waits for R1 · P1 waits for R2 · P2 waits for R3 · P3 waits for R0. No process can proceed, ever.
    
        
    
      
    

      
    
        
    Memory allocation & fragmentation
    
        
    One 1024-unit memory bar; the operating system itself occupies the first 128. Place processes with a placement policy and watch the holes. External fragmentation is computed live: total free memory that sits in holes too small to hold the next request is memory the system owns but cannot use — compaction fixes it by sliding every process together, at the cost of copying.
    
        
    
        
    
          
          
          
          
          
          
        
    
        
    
        
    Details — the three fits
          
    First-fit takes the first hole that fits (fast, tends to splinter the front). Best-fit takes the smallest hole that fits (leaves tiny slivers). Worst-fit takes the largest hole (keeps the remainder usable). None is always best — try placing 150, 300, 120, removing one, then placing 200 under each policy and compare the fragmentation readout.
    
        
    
      
    

      
    
        
    Address translation & TLB
    
        
    A 4 KB logical address space: 16 pages of 256 bytes, mapped by the page table below into a 64 KB physical memory (256 frames). Every translation checks the 4-entry TLB first (LRU); on a TLB miss the page table is walked in memory. Edit the page table, translate addresses, and watch the TLB fill — the effective access time is computed from your hit ratio and your timings.

    Segmentation variant (Advanced)
    
          
    Same address, different split: instead of page | offset, a segmented address is segment | offset and each segment has a base and a limit in a segment table. With segment table 0 → base 3000, limit 400 · 1 → base 6000, limit 250 · 2 → base 9000, limit 800, the top 2 bits of a 12-bit address pick the segment and the low 10 bits are the offset — checked against the limit before the base is added. Try it:
    
          
    
            
            
          
    
          
    0x4C8: segment 1, offset 0x0C8 = 200 — inside limit 250, so physical = 6000 + 200 = 6200.
